contentMarkdown:
# European Accessibility Act (EAA)

The European Accessibility Act (EAA) is an EU directive that sets accessibility requirements for certain products and services sold or provided in the EU. It covers consumer e-commerce, consumer banking, e-books, and specified digital aspects of passenger transport, among other services. The directive sets June 28, 2025, as the start date for applying national measures, with transition provisions for some cases.

## Which websites and apps does the EAA cover?

Scope depends on the service being offered. For e-commerce, the directive covers online services offered to consumers with a view to concluding a consumer contract. Websites and apps are channels through which those services can be offered. For websites and mobile apps of EU public sector bodies, see the Web Accessibility Directive and its relationship to [EN 301 549](/glossary/en-301-549.html).

Article 4(5) exempts microenterprises providing services. The definition in Article 3(23) uses fewer than 10 people and either annual turnover or an annual balance sheet total of no more than €2 million. The directive treats microenterprises dealing with products differently. Check the national implementing law and any relevant transition provisions for the service and country.

## What should a product team check in checkout?

For a travel site selling bookings to consumers, start with the real journey from fare selection to purchase confirmation. Test choosing a fare without a mouse, identifying errors in the traveler form, and completing payment authentication with assistive technology. Include payment or identity steps supplied by third parties in the evaluation. Annex I specifically addresses accessibility of identification, security, and payment functions provided as part of an e-commerce service.

## How does the EAA relate to WCAG and EN 301 549?

The EAA sets the legal requirements. [WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html) gives teams testable web criteria, and [EN 301 549](/glossary/en-301-549.html) covers a broader range of information and communication technology. Article 15 ties a presumption of conformity to requirements covered by standards or parts of standards referenced for the directive in the EU Official Journal. For an assessment, identify the applicable national law, Annex I requirements, and any references published for the EAA.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [EN 301 549](/glossary/en-301-549.html)
- [Web Accessibility Audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html)
- [ADA Web Accessibility](/glossary/ada-web-accessibility.html)

contentMarkdown:
# EN 301 549

EN 301 549 is a European technical standard for accessibility in information and communication technology (ICT). It covers web content, non-web documents, software, hardware, and services. Its web requirements draw on WCAG, and its other clauses address accessibility needs specific to different products and services.

## How does EN 301 549 relate to WCAG?

[WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html) provides testable requirements for accessible web content. EN 301 549 has separate clauses for web content, non-web documents, and software, as well as requirements for other areas such as documentation and support. If a service includes a downloadable PDF, for example, a team should assess the document as well as the page containing its download link.

## Which version of EN 301 549 applies?

Status checked in November 2026.

| Reference | What to check |
|---|---|
| **EN 301 549 v3.2.1 (2021)** | The harmonized reference cited for the EU Web Accessibility Directive. Its web criteria align with WCAG 2.1 Level AA. Use the applicable requirements identified for websites or mobile apps in Annex A. |
| **EN 301 549 v4.1.1 (2026)** | ETSI published this edition in September 2026. Its web requirements draw on WCAG 2.2 Level AA. Publication of the standard and citation in the EU Official Journal are separate steps. Check the Commission’s list for the directive you are applying. |
| **Contract or procurement** | Use the version and specific clauses named in the contract or tender. Confirm whether reports, documents, software, or support are in scope. |

The Web Accessibility Directive (Directive (EU) 2016/2102) covers websites and mobile apps of EU public sector bodies. It also requires an accessibility statement and a feedback mechanism. The [European Accessibility Act](/glossary/european-accessibility-act.html) has its own scope and process for recognizing harmonized references.

**Example.** For a municipal booking portal, document the exact version, include the complete booking journey, and check whether its downloadable confirmation is in scope. Record the applicable clause alongside each finding, even when the same issue also maps to a WCAG criterion.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [European Accessibility Act (EAA)](/glossary/european-accessibility-act.html)
- [Web Accessibility Audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html)
- [Section 508](/glossary/section-508.html)

# ADA Web Accessibility

ADA web accessibility refers to providing people with disabilities access to online services under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Title II applies to U.S. state and local government entities. Title III applies to businesses and nonprofits that qualify as places of public accommodation.

## How do Title II and Title III differ?

| ADA title | Web accessibility requirements |
|---|---|
| **Title II** | The U.S. Department of Justice rule sets WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the technical standard for covered web content and mobile apps that state and local governments provide or make available, including through relevant vendor arrangements. The rule specifies exceptions and other conditions. |
| **Title III** | The Department of Justice’s web guidance explains that covered public accommodations must make the goods and services they offer online accessible. Use WCAG as a technical benchmark and evaluate the obligations that apply to the business. |

## What are the ADA Title II web rule deadlines?

Under the April 2026 interim final rule, state and local government entities with a population of 50,000 or more, excluding special districts, have until **April 26, 2027**. Entities below 50,000 and special district governments have until **April 26, 2028**. Existing Title II obligations continue to apply before these dates.

## What should a product team do?

For a city’s online permit application, include the portal, its forms, and the submission and payment steps in the accessibility scope. Identify any applicable exceptions, then evaluate the covered process against WCAG 2.1 AA. For a private retailer, start with the scope of Title III and the applicable legal context. Use WCAG to turn barriers in browsing and checkout into testable findings. [Section 508](/glossary/section-508.html) is a separate federal ICT framework relevant to U.S. federal agencies and the products they procure.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [Section 508](/glossary/section-508.html)
- [Web Accessibility Audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html)
- [European Accessibility Act (EAA)](/glossary/european-accessibility-act.html)

## Sources

- [ADA Title III Regulations, U.S. Department of Justice](https://www.ada.gov/law-and-regs/regulations/title-iii-regulations/)

contentMarkdown:
# Section 508

Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act requires U.S. federal agencies to make covered information and communication technology (ICT) accessible when they develop, procure, maintain, or use it. The Revised Section 508 Standards cover areas such as websites, electronic documents, software, hardware, and support documentation.

## Which WCAG version does Section 508 use?

The Revised Section 508 Standards incorporate **WCAG 2.0 Level AA (including Level A)** for covered electronic content under E205.4 and for covered software under E207.2, with specified exceptions for some non-web criteria. Additional ICT requirements can apply. Teams using WCAG 2.2 for their own product work should still map evidence to the criteria and clauses the procurement names.

## What are VPATs and ACRs?

An **Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR)** describes how a specific product or version meets applicable accessibility requirements. A **VPAT** is a template vendors can use to prepare that report. An ACR supports procurement review, and its scope and test evidence determine how much the buyer can infer about a real workflow.

## Example: A SaaS tool for a federal agency

A federal agency evaluating a case-management app might request an ACR for the version under consideration. The product team can document keyboard access to the case table, screen reader output for status changes, and the accessibility of generated reports. The agency can review the evidence against the procurement’s requirements and test a representative workflow. Record the product version, test scope, and limitations with enough detail for the agency to assess their impact.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)

- [EN 301 549](/glossary/en-301-549.html)

contentMarkdown:
# Web Accessibility Audit

A web accessibility audit is a documented evaluation of a website or web app against a defined accessibility standard and scope. It identifies barriers, records how they were found, and gives teams evidence they can use to prioritize fixes and verify changes.

## How do you run a web accessibility audit?

1. **Define the scope and target.** Record the site or release, WCAG version and level or other applicable standard, and the browsers and assistive technologies used for testing.
2. **Sample representative content and complete tasks.** Include common templates, shared components, different states, and critical journeys such as checkout. If a sampled page is part of a process, include the steps needed to complete that process.
3. **Combine automated and manual tests.** Use scans for issues they can identify. Test keyboard operation, focus order, zoom and reflow, labels, errors, and announcements by hand. Include people with disabilities in usability evaluation to understand how barriers affect real tasks.
4. **Report and retest.** Record the affected page or state, environment, steps to reproduce, expected behavior, actual result, user impact, and applicable criterion. Retest the fix across other instances of a shared component.

## Example: A keyboard trap during checkout

| Evidence | Example finding |
|---|---|
| Location and test | Checkout, payment-help dialog. Open it by keyboard and try to close it with the available controls. |
| Actual result and impact | Focus stays inside the dialog. The visible close icon only responds to pointer input, so a keyboard user cannot return to payment. |
| Criterion and fix | WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A). Make the close control keyboard-operable and verify that focus returns to the trigger when the dialog closes. |

The report should identify what the sample covers and any areas that remain untested. A short check of one page can uncover barriers. A conformance evaluation requires a broader review of the defined scope.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [Semantic HTML](/glossary/semantic-html.html)
- [ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)](/glossary/aria-accessible-rich-internet-applications.html)
- [EN 301 549](/glossary/en-301-549.html)
